searches.note: Nineteen searches of a share of twenty eight, nine left unspent for the run's shared allowance; the GG dryness rule (one search) serves two records and is counted with Emrich-Schönleber, one wasted search returned nothing on Schäfer-Fröhlich and is counted with it, two on Gut Hermannsberg returned nothing. Most were restricted to the VDP's, wein.plus's or a house's own domain and read as summaries. Writers' own sites that came up were read and never cited. No fetch tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites with their heights and aspects, the making, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the dates the stories turn on (Dönnhoff's 1750, 1971 and 2007; Emrich-Schönleber's 1994; Schäfer-Fröhlich's 1995 and 2001; Gut Hermannsberg's 1901, 1902, 1946, 1998 and 2009 and the five year release; Diel's 1802, 1989 and February 2023; the VDP's 2006 dryness rule), then to the sites' heights, aspects and soils on the VDP's own pages, then to the others.

Where sources disagreed on a year (the state's takeover of the Nahe domain, 1946 or 1950) the year was taken out and the question re-keyed on what both agree; where a claim rested on nothing read (the Felsenberg's vessels, the Burgberg's soil, the river between Oberhausen and the Hermannshöhle) it was cut or narrowed; where a house's range did not hold a wine (Dönnhoff's Kupfergrube) it was replaced from the house's own lists.

tested: The family's dates: 1750 against the house's press piece, which has the family's records begin in 1761 with a chronicle of 1781 and 1784; Wikipedia gives 1750. Both kept, as the story already says.

1971: the son took on the parents' estate from his father Hermann, whose name it carries, confirmed on the house's own press piece and on Wikipedia. 2007: the son of the next generation responsible for the wines for fourteen years in December 2021, on the house's press piece.

The Hermannshöhle on the VDP's page and the house's sheets: 130 to 175 metres, S to SW, 40 to 70 per cent, black grey weathered slate with volcanic rock, limestone and porphyry, the Nahe's reference site for over a century. The aspect was due south in the record; corrected.
The parcels bought from a former VDP Nahe chairman: the house's own press piece; no year.

The Oberhäuser Brücke as the house's monopole beside the Luitpoldbrücke, the source of Spätlese, Auslese and Eiswein: Skurnik and the house's sheets. Whether the Hermannshöhle lies across the river from Oberhausen was not borne out by anything read, so the wording now says the neighbouring village.

The others against the house's price lists and shop: Hermannshöhle, Dellchen, Felsenberg Felsentürmchen, Krötenpfuhl, Höllenpfad im Mühlenberg and Brücke appear; no Kupfergrube GG does, so it was replaced.
The VDP's release rule (1 September of the year after the harvest) and the legal dryness of GG from the 2006 vintage by the VDP's own statement.

The questions: one right answer each, options of one kind; the story question's distractors 1750 and 2007 are the record's own dates and teach. House rules: no living name, no price, no score, British, no dash.

tested: The Halenberg on the VDP's page: east of Monzingen, 160 to 220 metres, 20 to 70 per cent, south to south west, weathered Waderner Schichten, a conglomerate of blue grey slate and quartzite. The record's south south west widened to the VDP's range.
VDP admission in 1994: wein.plus, beside the author's Sommelier Academy; 2001 for Schäfer-Fröhlich and 1989 for Diel, the distractors of the story question, both confirmed on the VDP's own pages.

The family's vines since the middle of the eighteenth century and the turn to a pure wine estate between 1965 and 1985: wein.plus and a second guide give the mid eighteenth century and the 1960s start; the 1965 to 1985 span is in two results.
The legal dryness of GG from the 2006 vintage: the VDP's own statement, read through two summaries; GG as a dry wine defined in 2002 (wein.plus magazine).

The questions: the wine question's distractors are the soils of other Nahe sites in this group and teach; the story question's three wrong years are the other houses' admissions. House rules: the living father and sons are not named.

tested: The VDP's estate page: admitted in 2001, the cellar in the son's hands since the 1995 vintage, the Felseneck and the Stromberg at Bockenau held alone. All borne out.

The Felseneck on the VDP's page: 250 to 310 metres, 35 to 70 per cent, due south, soils dominated by Upper Rotliegend with Devonian slate, quartzite and basalt rubble; wein.plus gives 200 to 300 metres and a blue Devonian slate conglomerate in the Ellerbach valley. The record follows the VDP for height and aspect and names the soils both give.
The upper Nahe: no source read places the Ellerbach valley in the upper valley, so the word was taken out of place, sites and table.
The wine question's explanation contradicted the record's own basalt scree by calling the Felseneck no volcanic site; rewritten.
Spontaneous fermentation as the source of the struck match reduction: the house's own words on the VDP page and two merchants, as the author read them; not refuted.

tested: The founding: 1902 on the house's history and lexicon and Wines of Germany; one summary has the mine stop and the land pass to Prussia in 1901. Kept at 1902, open.
The copper mine worked until 1901, the terraces cut with convict labour and the first vintage of 1907: the house and wein.plus. The story's some years later stands.

The state after the war: one account gives 1946, the house's own lexicon 1950 (when it became the Nahe State Domain). Neither year can stand, so the story and the question now say after the Second World War.
The privatisation of 1998 and the sale of 2009: the house's own history page and wein.plus, several accounts. The buyers of 2009 are living and not named.

The Kupfergrube held back for five years: release moved from two years to five after the harvest, the 2017 vintage released on 1 September 2022, a partial hold back of the 2015 before it, and the bottling labelled Reserve. The record's a vintage of the middle 2010s stands.
The Felsenberg's note on vessels was found in nothing read and was cut.

tested: 1802: the house's own pages and wein.plus, which names the buyer Johann Peter Diel (1750 to 1811), during the Napoleonic occupation; one source only for the name and dates, so the story keeps a forebear.
VDP admission in 1989: the house and the VDP's own listing.
The Verband traditioneller Sektmacher: the house's own press page of 16 February 2023 quotes the unanimous admission. Borne out.

The Goldloch on the VDP's page: 140 to 210 metres, 15 to 55 per cent, rocky loam slope wash and a thin pebbly loam over Upper Rotliegend conglomerate, facing south or south south west; wein.plus agrees on the soil and gives other heights. The record's aspect widened.
The making in native yeasts and old Stückfass casks of local oak: the house's page for the 2024 GG, as the author read it; not refuted.
The story set the Goldloch against both other sites as not slate; the Burgberg's soil was not read, so it now names the Pittermännchen alone.

swaps.proposed: none; the author invited a swap of the Goldloch GG for the Pittermännchen GG
swaps.why: No source found ranks either above the other: the house presents its three Dorsheim Grosse Lage wines as equals, the Goldloch carries the plan's key and is as well known for its Prädikat wines and its Sekt, and the Pittermännchen stands first among the others, so the guest meets both.

swapNote: No other swap was proposed. Plan notes answered: Dönnhoff's 1750 is in two sources beside wein.plus's 1761; the Hermannshöhle's soils are the VDP's and the house's; the Halenberg's soils are the VDP's in two pages; the Felseneck's soil is named only where the VDP and wein.plus agree, the Kupfergrube in others; Gut Hermannsberg's 1902 and the mine to 1901 are the house's and wein.plus's, the holding back is told as a habit begun in the middle 2010s; Diel's Goldloch kept, with the Pittermännchen first among the others.
